quotes.citation: A Plain Account of Christian Perfection (1766), §§19, 25 (paraphrase)

quotes.text: Phoebe Palmer taught a "shorter way": lay all on the altar, which is Christ, believe God’s promise that the altar sanctifies the gift, and testify to entire sanctification now rather than waiting for feelings.
Hannah Whitall Smith urges believers to stop striving and to hand over the whole of life to Christ in full consecration, trusting him moment by moment to live the victorious life in them.
quotes.citation: The Christian’s Secret of a Happy Life (1875) (paraphrase)

quotes.text: Durham argued that the believer is sanctified in Christ at conversion by the finished work of Calvary; there is no second crisis of cleansing, only an ongoing appropriation of what was already given.

Hodges holds that eternal life is given freely to anyone who believes Jesus’ promise of it; to require surrender, perseverance or fruit as conditions of salvation or of assurance would turn grace into a reward.
MacArthur argues that the gospel Jesus preached calls sinners to repentance and to submit to him as Lord; a "faith" that leaves life unchanged is not the saving faith of the New Testament.

Sanders argues that in Palestinian Judaism one "gets in" to the covenant by God’s gracious election and "stays in" by obedience and atonement — a pattern he calls covenantal nomism, not legalistic earning of salvation.

Wright argues that for Paul justification is God’s declaration of who belongs to his single worldwide covenant family, marked by faith in Jesus, anticipating the final verdict that will accord with the whole life lived in the Spirit.
quotes.citation: What Saint Paul Really Said (1997); Justification (2009) (paraphrase)

quotes.text: For He was made man that we might be made God; and He manifested Himself by a body that we might receive the idea of the unseen Father; and He endured the insolence of men that we might inherit immortality.
Our Lord Jesus Christ, who did, through His transcendent love, become what we are, that He might bring us to be even what He is Himself.
quotes.translation: tr. A. Roberts & W. Rambaut, ANF 1 (1885)

quotes.text: For the glory of God is a living man; and the life of man consists in beholding God.
quotes.translation: tr. A. Roberts & W. Rambaut, ANF 1 (1885)

quotes.text: Palamas teaches that God is wholly present in his uncreated energies, so that the saints truly participate in God and become gods by grace, while God’s essence remains utterly beyond participation and knowledge.
quotes.citation: Triads III.2-3; One Hundred and Fifty Chapters 75-81 (paraphrase)

quotes.text: For the end is always like the beginning.
quotes.translation: tr. Frederick Crombie, ANF 4 (1885), from Rufinus’ Latin

quotes.text: Origen reasons from 1 Corinthians 15:24-28 that when Christ subjects all things to the Father, his enemies are conquered not by destruction but by correction, so that God may be "all in all".

In the dialogue Macrina argues that evil has no existence of its own and so cannot last forever; the fire of judgement purifies like a refiner’s fire until evil is wholly removed and God is all in all.
quotes.citation: On the Soul and the Resurrection (paraphrase)

quotes.text: Isaac of Nineveh teaches that those in Gehenna are scourged by the scourge of love, and in his later homilies hopes that the mercy which created all things will not be defeated in the end.
quotes.citation: Ascetical Homilies I.28; Second Part, Homilies 39-41 (paraphrase)

quotes.text: All shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well.
quotes.citation: Revelations of Divine Love, ch. 27 (Thirteenth Revelation)

quotes.text: Talbott argues that a God of perfect love would never cease seeking the lost, and that since no fully informed person could have a motive to reject the source of their own happiness forever, God’s love will in the end win everyone freely.
Hart contends that a God who creates freely out of nothing is morally responsible for the final end of all he makes, so that eternal torment would make God’s goodness unintelligible.
Fudge argues that the Bible’s language of death, destruction and consuming fire means that the unsaved finally perish; immortality is God’s gift in Christ, not a natural possession of every soul.

Stott wrote that he held the view tentatively, but found it emotionally intolerable and exegetically unpersuasive that people could be kept in conscious torment for ever; he judged final annihilation a legitimate, biblically founded alternative.
quotes.citation: Essentials: A Liberal-Evangelical Dialogue (with David L. Edwards, 1988), pp. 312-320 (paraphrase)

quotes.text: The God that holds you over the pit of hell, much as one holds a spider, or some loathsome insect, over the fire, abhors you, and is dreadfully provoked.
quotes.citation: Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God (Enfield, 8 July 1741)

people.name: Caesarius of Arles
people.summary: Bishop of Arles (502-542), popular preacher and monastic legislator, who presided over the Second Council of Orange (529) that settled the semi-Pelagian controversy in favour of a moderate Augustinianism.

people.name: David Bentley Hart
people.summary: American Orthodox theologian and translator of the New Testament (2017) whose That All Shall Be Saved (2019) argues that eternal torment is incompatible with God as creator ex nihilo and perfect goodness.
keyIdeas: Classical theism and the goodness of God

people.name: E. P. Sanders
people.summary: American scholar whose Paul and Palestinian Judaism (1977) argued that Second Temple Judaism was a religion of grace ("covenantal nomism"), not legalistic works-righteousness, launching what became the New Perspective on Paul.

people.name: Hannah Whitall Smith
people.summary: American Quaker-born Holiness writer whose The Christian’s Secret of a Happy Life (1875), with the Brighton and Oxford conventions she and her husband Robert Pearsall Smith led, helped launch the Keswick "higher life" movement.

people.name: Isaac of Nineveh (Isaac the Syrian)
people.summary: Seventh-century monk of the Church of the East, briefly bishop of Nineveh, whose ascetic homilies were translated into Greek and loved across Orthodox Christendom; in his "Second Part" he expressed the hope that Gehenna is remedial and that God’s love will finally prevail for all.
keyIdeas: Gehenna as the scourge of love

people.name: James D. G. Dunn
people.summary: British New Testament scholar (Durham) who named the "New Perspective on Paul" (1982 Manson lecture), arguing that "works of the law" refers chiefly to Jewish boundary markers; his Baptism in the Holy Spirit (1970) argued that Spirit-baptism in the New Testament is part of conversion-initiation.

people.name: John Cassian
people.summary: Monk trained among the Desert Fathers of Egypt who founded monasteries at Marseille; his Conferences (c.426-429), especially Conference 13, held that the first movement toward God can arise from the human will, assisted by grace — a view later labelled "semi-Pelagian". He is venerated as a saint in East and West.
keyIdeas: Desert spirituality transmitted to the West

people.name: John Gill
people.summary: English Particular Baptist pastor in Southwark and learned commentator; often associated with "high" or hyper-Calvinism for teaching eternal justification and reluctance to offer the gospel indiscriminately, though scholars debate how far he denied the free offer.

people.name: John MacArthur
people.summary: Pastor of Grace Community Church, Sun Valley, California, whose The Gospel According to Jesus (1988) argued that saving faith includes submission to Christ as Lord, sparking the "lordship salvation" debate.

people.name: Luis de Molina
people.summary: Spanish Jesuit whose Concordia (1588) reconciled grace, foreknowledge and free will through God’s "middle knowledge" (scientia media) of what free creatures would do in any circumstance; this provoked the De Auxiliis controversy with the Dominicans.

people.name: Moïse Amyraut
people.summary: French Huguenot theologian at the Academy of Saumur whose Brief Traitté de la prédestination (1634), developing John Cameron, taught a "hypothetical universalism": Christ died for all on condition of faith, while God elects some to receive faith.
keyIdeas: Universal conditional decree prior to particular election

people.name: Thomas Talbott
people.summary: American philosopher (Willamette University) whose The Inescapable Love of God (1999) argued on biblical and philosophical grounds that God’s love will eventually win every person freely.

people.name: William H. Durham
people.summary: Chicago pastor baptized in the Spirit at Azusa Street (1907) who in 1910 preached "the Finished Work of Calvary": sanctification is received at conversion by identification with Christ and then progressively appropriated, rejecting a separate second work of entire sanctification.

people.name: Zane C. Hodges
people.summary: Dallas Theological Seminary professor and co-founder of the Grace Evangelical Society (1986), leading exponent of "free grace" theology: eternal life is received by believing Jesus’ promise, without requiring commitment to his lordship or evidence of fruit.
keyIdeas: Assurance from the promise, not from works

works.title: Confessions
works.summary: Augustine's autobiographical prayer to God, narrating his restless search, his conversion in the garden at Milan (386) and meditations on memory, time and creation.
works.significance: Its prayer "give what you command" provoked Pelagius; it became the model of Christian autobiography and of grace experienced as rescue.

works.title: Enchiridion on Faith, Hope and Love
works.summary: A short handbook of the faith organised around the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, written for a layman named Laurentius.
works.significance: A compact summary of Augustine's mature theology of sin, grace and predestination.

works.title: On Nature and Grace (De natura et gratia)
works.summary: Augustine's reply to Pelagius' lost treatise On Nature. He argues that human nature, created good, has been wounded by Adam's sin so that it cannot be healed or fulfil the law without the grace of Christ, which is not merely teaching or example but an inner healing power.
works.significance: The first full anti-Pelagian answer that names Pelagius directly; it fixed the Western framing of nature and grace for a millennium.

works.title: Canons of the Second Council of Orange
works.author: Council of Orange (Arausio), presided over by Caesarius of Arles
works.summary: Twenty-five canons and a conclusion, drawn largely from Augustine and Prosper of Aquitaine, affirming that even the beginning of faith is a gift of grace, while rejecting predestination to evil.
works.significance: Defined a moderate Augustinianism against "semi-Pelagianism"; confirmed by Pope Boniface II in 531, then largely forgotten until rediscovered in the 16th century.

works.title: Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God
works.summary: Sermon preached at Enfield, Connecticut, on 8 July 1741 on Deuteronomy 32:35, depicting the precariousness of the unconverted.
works.significance: The most famous sermon of the First Great Awakening and an emblem of the doctrine of eternal punishment in American memory.

works.title: On the Soul and the Resurrection
works.summary: A dialogue modelled on Plato's Phaedo between Gregory and his dying sister Macrina on death, resurrection and the purifying end of evil.
works.significance: Principal source for Gregory's hope of universal restoration.

works.title: Revelations of Divine Love
works.summary: Julian’s account and long meditation on sixteen "showings" received in May 1373, including the assurance that "all shall be well".
works.significance: The first book in English known to be written by a woman; a touchstone for later hopeful eschatologies.

works.title: The Bondage of the Will (De servo arbitrio)
works.summary: Luther's reply to Erasmus' Diatribe on Free Will (1524), arguing that the fallen will is bound in matters of salvation and that God's foreknowledge and will are immutable.
works.significance: Luther considered it, with the Catechism, among his few books worth preserving; it marked the break between humanism and the Reformation.

works.title: The Freedom of a Christian (De libertate christiana)
works.summary: Luther's short treatise, sent with a letter to Pope Leo X, arguing that faith alone justifies, unites the soul with Christ like a bride with a bridegroom (the 'joyful exchange'), and then freely overflows in love to the neighbour.
works.significance: The most widely read summary of Reformation soteriology; it holds forensic justification and union with Christ together.

works.title: Triads in Defence of the Holy Hesychasts
works.summary: Three sets of three treatises defending hesychast prayer against Barlaam of Calabria, arguing that the saints truly participate in God’s uncreated energies (as in the light of Tabor) while God’s essence remains imparticipable.
works.significance: Source of the essence/energies distinction endorsed by the Constantinople councils of 1341-1351.

works.title: Letter to Demetrias (Epistula ad Demetriadem)
works.summary: A spiritual letter to the young Roman aristocrat Demetrias on her taking the veil, urging her that God commands nothing impossible and that human nature, as created by God, is capable of holiness.
works.significance: The most complete surviving statement of Pelagius' own teaching (long transmitted under the names of Jerome and Augustine).

works.title: Smalcald Articles
works.summary: Articles drawn up by Luther for a proposed general council, distinguishing points that can and cannot be yielded; the "first and chief article" is justification through Christ.
works.significance: Part of the Lutheran Book of Concord (1580).

works.title: Journal of John Wesley
works.summary: Wesley's published journal (1735-1790), including the Aldersgate entry of 24 May 1738 describing his assurance of forgiveness.
works.significance: A primary source for the Evangelical Revival and for the Methodist doctrine of assurance.

works.title: A Plain Account of Christian Perfection
works.summary: Wesley's account of his teaching on Christian perfection (entire sanctification): love filling the heart and excluding sin, received by faith, often instantaneously, yet always growing.
works.significance: Charter text of the Methodist and later Holiness doctrine of entire sanctification.
